source.title: Binary Sparse Coding for Interpretability
source.authors: Lucia Quirke; Stepan Shabalin; Nora Belrose

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares binary and continuous sparse coders and evaluates their feature interpretability using auto-interpretability scores, rather than measuring individual neurons with the original neuron-visualization method.
record.gate_note: The results concern sparse-autoencoder/transcoder features in SmolLM2, not the base model's individual neurons. The paper's introductory statements about neuron polysemanticity and cited findings are not results from this study. Sparse-probing results and the Figure 8 comparison of interpretability score with causal effect do not measure the claim versions. Several figure-only comparisons are included with values left as figure only.
record.test_reason: The study proposes binary sparse autoencoders and transcoders, then reports their interpretability, loss and probing performance against continuous coders on SmolLM2. Every result concerns features of a sparse coder, an interpretability tool, not the base model's neurons. No version measures this. V5 concerns how the network's own activation function or architecture changes the share of polysemantic neurons. V7 concerns how neurons get classified as polysemantic. The binary-versus-TopK comparison is a related construct on sparse-coder features, so it is recorded under fits_no_version. The statement that most neurons are polysemantic is cited ([2],[12]), not measured.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors find that binarisation raises unweighted feature interpretability but raises loss and variance unexplained. It also produces uninterpretable ultra-high-frequency features, so frequency-adjusted scores slightly favour continuous coders. They do not recommend binary coders for most purposes. They take this as support that polysemanticity may be ineliminable, while stating they cannot prove it. Binary coders did better on sparse probing after finetuning.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains binary sparse autoencoders/transcoders and compares their feature interpretability with continuous sparse coders; it does not reproduce the original neuron-level visualization or feature-identification method.
record.method_sensitivity: Interpretability comparisons differ between unweighted and frequency-weighted scores; observed feature contexts vary by activation decile; scores can overestimate interpretability when negative examples are randomly rather than adversarially selected. Binary versus continuous coding and the tested coder/model settings also change results.

fits_no_version.finding: Binarising sparse-coder activations raises unweighted auto-interp F1 on SmolLM2-135M. With frequency weighting there is no gain, and continuous coders score slightly better. Binarisation also creates uninterpretable ultra-high-frequency features and raises patched loss. The single-seed 1.7B run shows binary higher on all four metrics.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Constraining sparse-coder features to binary values shifts polysemanticity from low activation strengths into high-frequency features rather than removing it.

fits_no_version.finding: An SAE feature is coherent in its top seven activation deciles but fires in diverse contexts in lower deciles. A feature with perfect auto-interp scores still has clear non-activating counterexamples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Judgements of whether SAE features are monosemantic depend on the activation range examined and on how negative examples are chosen in scoring.

record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2025 (39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems)
record.problems: Results are based on sparse-coder features from a sample of the SmolLM2 training corpus, not individual neurons. The authors note a single dataset, dead neurons in some coders, and possible changes at larger widths. The SmolLM2-1.7B comparison is a single-seed run. Several comparisons are only presented in figures without extractable numerical values. The paper also notes that random negative examples can make interpretability scores overestimate feature interpretability.
record.rows_left_out: No result rows were made for Table 1 sparse probing, because it measures concept probing performance rather than polysemanticity or its interpretability measurement. Figure 8's feature-bin ablation results concern the relation between interpretability score and causal effect, not a claim version. Other cited results are not results from this study.

untested.parts: All of it: no vision models.
All of it: no measurement of model MLP neurons. The prevalence statement is cited.
The model's own activation function or architecture and its effect on the share of polysemantic neurons. Only the sparse-coder activation is varied.
Neuron-level classification. Activation-range and scoring dependence are shown only for SAE features.

record.verdict_notes: All results concern sparse-coder features, not neurons, so no version receives a verdict. The single-seed 1.7B Table 2 (binary better even frequency-weighted) conflicts with the 135M frequency-weighted result and the abstract's summary. The 'ineliminable polysemanticity' conclusion is a hypothesis about SAE features, not a measurement of neurons.

versions.untested_parts: Image-classifier neurons and the InceptionV1 examples.
The prevalence of polysemantic MLP neurons in transformer language models, including token/context mixtures and layer-wise shares.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by superposition or by a feature-to-neuron capacity imbalance.
Polysemanticity caused by initialization, regularization, or training noise when capacity is sufficient.

The study tests binary versus continuous sparse coders and their interpretability/performance tradeoff, but does not test modern convnets or establish that the compared feature scores are the share of polysemantic neurons.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons, including neuron 4e:55, detect a shared feature or related jobs.
The study examines activation deciles, frequency adjustment, and auto-interpretability scoring for sparse-coder features, not alternative explanation methods for individual neurons.

reader_labels.reason: Binary coders match or outperform continuous coders on unweighted fuzzing F1 in the 135M sweep (R1), and have higher reported F1 scores on all four Table 2 metrics in the single-seed 1.7B comparison (R3–R6).

reader_labels.reason: The 135M results say frequency-weighted fuzzing scores are often lower for binary coders (R2), ultra-high-frequency uninterpretable features are more common (R12), and binarization increases loss when patched into the model (R7).

reader_labels.label: supports
